knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",

This vignette recomputes the main design numbers of Halkiewicz and Alexeev,
*Concurrent controls and heterogeneity tolerance in stepped-wedge trials*
(arXiv:2610.35853).

A design is written as cluster counts for start periods `2, ..., T`, followed
by the number of wait-listed clusters (never treated during follow-up). With
24 clusters and five periods, the balanced complete wedge is `c(6, 6, 6, 6, 0)`.

```{r}
library(panelcert)
designs <- list(complete = c(6, 6, 6, 6, 0), wait4 = c(5, 5, 5, 5, 4),
                wait8 = c(4, 4, 4, 4, 8), wait12 = c(3, 3, 3, 3, 12),
                capped_opt = c(6, 6, 1, 0, 11))
```

## Exposure weights and the adequacy radius

The conventional immediate-treatment (IT) estimator averages the
exposure-specific effects with weights `W`. The adequacy radius `kappa*` is the
RMS exposure-time heterogeneity, relative to the planned effect, that the IT
analysis tolerates before worst-case coverage of its 95% interval falls to 90%
(planned power 80%).

```{r}
round(sw_exposure_weights(designs$complete, phi = 2), 3)
sapply(designs, function(d) round(sw_radius(design = d, phi = 2), 3))
```

The complete wedge tolerates heterogeneity of only about 13% of the planned
effect, and wait-listing raises the radius.

## Cost of the estimand-aligned analysis

The exposure-time-indicator (ETI) analysis targets the time-averaged
treatment effect directly. Its cost is its variance relative to the IT variance
of the complete wedge.

```{r}
t(sapply(designs, function(d) {
  ec <- sw_eti_cost(d, phi = 2)
  round(c(eti_cost = ec$eti_cost, it_ratio = ec$it_ratio), 2)
}))
```

For a fixed rollout shape, the ETI variance first falls and then rises with the
wait-list share (Theorem 3 of the paper).

```{r}
q <- seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.05)
cost <- sapply(q, function(x) sw_eti_cost(c(rep((1 - x) / 4, 4), x), phi = 2)$eti_cost)
round(cbind(q, cost), 2)[c(1, 5, 8, 9, 11, 17), ]
```

## Rollout-capped design search

At most six clusters may start in any period. The frontier gives the smallest
ETI cost for each bound on the number wait-listed.

```{r}
s <- sw_design_search(G = 24, T = 5, cap = 6, max_wait = 12, phi = 2)
s$frontier[s$frontier$max_wait %in% c(0, 4, 6, 8, 12), ]
```

## Nested-exchangeable correlation and unequal cluster sizes

Under nested-exchangeable correlation, every result holds with the effective
parameter `phi'`. With an ICC of 0.05, cluster autocorrelation 0.5 and 20
individuals per cluster-period:

```{r}
sw_phi_nested(icc = 0.05, cac = 0.5, m = 20)
sw_radius(design = designs$complete, icc = 0.05, cac = 0.5, m = 20)
```

The bundled weekend allied-health trial (`haines2017`; CC BY 4.0) has unequal
ward-period sizes. Its IT exposure weights at the actual cell sizes, under the
fitted intracluster correlation 0.0709, give a radius of 0.124.

```{r}
n <- with(haines2017, tapply(rep(1, nrow(haines2017)), list(ward, period), sum))
starts <- tapply(haines2017$start, haines2017$ward, `[`, 1)
ord <- order(starts, as.numeric(names(starts)))
W <- sw_exposure_weights(c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 0), icc = 0.0709, cac = 1,
                         sizes = n[ord, ])
round(W, 3)
round(sw_radius(W), 4)
```
